title: Ardas before a journey
hookLine: before travel, exams or new work, Sikhs ask for help in Ardas

cards: The suitcase is zipped. The ride is two minutes away. A student has an exam at nine; someone starts a new job on Monday and hasn't slept well all weekend.

In some Sikh families, before anyone walks out, hands fold and a short Ardas is said, sometimes by a grandparent, sometimes by the traveler. Sometimes the family goes to the gurdwara first and asks for the Ardas there.
Then, and only then, the door opens.

teach.b: Every full Ardas already asks for this. Near the end comes the line sarbat de kaaraj raas karne: make everyone's tasks succeed. Kaaraj is a task, an undertaking.
Raas means set right, brought to a good end. It's a general request, for everybody.
Before a journey, an exam, a wedding, a surgery or a new business, Sikhs make it specific: this trip, this test, this first day.
Families sometimes offer karah prashad at the gurdwara so the Ardas can be said there, with the congregation joining in. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib fits these moments.

teach.h: SPEAK OF IT TO THE LORD.
teach.b: In Sri Rag ki Var, on ang 91, it says, in effect: whatever work you want done, speak of it to the Lord; the True Guru will set it right, and you have His word on it. Notice what this asking isn't.
It isn't a lucky charm, and it isn't a way to skip the studying. Sikh teaching expects honest effort: you still pack, still prepare, still drive carefully.
In the Ardas, effort and outcome come in order: the work is done, the result is placed in the hands of the One, and then the traveler goes.
And saying a task out loud means naming what you're really walking into: this is the road, this is what I hope for, this is in Your hands.

how: Before travel, exams, a new job or another undertaking, Sikhs often say a short Ardas at home or ask for one at the gurdwara, sometimes offering karah prashad, asking that the task be brought to a good end.

games.q: you're leaving for a long trip in five minutes. your grandmother stops you at the door. what's she likely to ask?
o: a short Ardas before you go.
games.why: the Ardas doesn't replace packing. the work comes first, then the result is placed in the hands of the One.

practice: Think of your very next real task, a call, a drive, a meeting, and picture the doorway you'll cross to get to it. On the in-breath, see yourself doing the work honestly and well; on the out-breath, let go of how it turns out.
If you pray, you can place it before the One in your own words, or simply say Waheguru.
